list.listitem: Patients with hyperkalemia who are clinically unstable require urgent admission to the critical care unit for immediate reduction of their serum potassium. C
Intravenous calcium provides immediate correction of life-threatening hyperkalemia, such as that accompanied by ECG changes. C
Potassium-binding agents (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer, or sodium polystyrene sulfonate) may be used to remove potassium from the body, depending on clinical setting and availability. B
In addition, they require treatment with a faster acting agent, such as inhaled beta agonists, insulin-glucose, or both. B

background.definition: Hyperkalemia is defined as a serum potassium more than two standard deviations from the mean. In most laboratories, this will be a serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/dL. Values over 6.0 mEq/dL can lead to fatal arrhythmias, especially if the increase in potassium is rapid. If the increase is gradual, even levels over 7.0 mEq/dL can be tolerated.

list.listitem: Between 1% and 10% of hospitalized patients.
Community prevalence and incidence are not known.

Medications: angiontensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, direct renin inhibitors such as aliskirin, angiotensin receptor blockers, eplerenone, NSAIDs, amiloride, potassium supplements, triamterene, spironolactone, tacrolimus, trimethoprim, beta-blockers.

In a 21-month follow-up study of 2737 heart failure patients on on standard heart failure therapy in whom eplerenone was added, 32.5% developed serum potassium levels greater that 5.0 mmol/L, and 8.9% developed serum potassium levels >5.5 mmol/L.
Among 3445 patients with heart failure but preserved ejection fraction using spironolactone, the rate of hyperkalemia was 18.7% over 3.3 years. This was double the rate of patients on placebo.

In a meta-analysis of seven trials of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy (MRA) in patients after a myocardial infarction or with chronic heart failure (16,065 patients), hyperkalemia was observed in approximately 9.3% of those on MRA therapy versus 4.3% of those on placebo. However only 54% of those on MRA therapy were deemed to have MRA-associated hyperkalemia, and 46% of the cases were non-MRA related.
Renal failure.
Acute tissue injury.
Hyperosmolar states such as diabetic ketoacidosis.
Insulin deficiency or resistance.
Adrenal disease.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Hyporenenemic hypoaldosteronism.
Systemic lupus erythematosis.
Type IV renal tubular acidosis.
Pseudohyperkalemia resulting from drawing blood in the same arm in which potassium is being infused, hemolysis, or laboratory error.
Excess potassium intake.
Decreased renal excretion of potassium resulting from medications.
Movement of potassium out of cells into the blood stream as a result of acidosis or medications.
Patients with risk factors for hyperkalemia and symptoms such as weakness, mental changes, or ileus should have serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine determined. C
Once hyperkalemia is diagnosed, an electrocardiogram and a spot urine for potassium, sodium, creatinine, and measured osmolarity should be obtained. C
Patients with hyperkalemia are usually asymptomatic but may present with weakness or mental status changes.

Patients may be discovered after routine laboratory studies, or because of typical ECG changes such as QT interval shortening, peaked T waves, or nodal or ventricular arrhythmias. In more acute cases, the ECG shows QRS complex widening, PR interval prolongation, and, with very high levels, absent P waves.
The history is directed toward finding underlying causes, in particular predisposing medications or illnesses such as diabetes, renal failure, or adrenal insufficiency.
Consideration for adrenal insufficiency should be present in patients with otherwise unexplained symptoms including hypotension, hyponatremia, volume depletion, hypoglycemia and /or hyperkalemia.
A diet history shuld be obtained to identify any potassium-containing foods or supplements.

However, in a clinical trial in 20 hypertensive subjects with normal renal function treated with an ACEi or ARB, random assignment to a high potassum diet (~5215 mg/d) was not associated with a significant increase in serum potassium compared to baseline or compared to thise with random assignment to a usual diet.
Obtain serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and glucose if hyperkalemia is suspected.
If hyperkalemia is confirmed, obtain a venous or arterial pH, urine for sodium, potassium, creatinine, and a measured (not calculated) urine osmolarity.

ECG findings consistent with hyperkalemia such as tall, peaked T waves, absent P waves, or widened QRS complexes indicate a heightened risk of arrythmias associated with hyperkalemia and may merit intensive care admission. However, arrythmias can occur even when the ECG is normal, especially if the rise in serum potassium is acute rather than gradual.
Acidosis (low serum pH) is a significant risk factor for arrhythmias.

If adrenal insufficiency is suspect in a patient with hyperkalemia, an IV corticotropin test should be considered. A peak cortisol level of 18 mcg/dL at 30 or 60 minutes is diagnostic for adrenal insufficiency.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management of hyperkalemia.

Patients with hyperkalemia who have acidosis, an apparent rapid rise in serum potassium rather than a gradual one, significant symptoms, or ECG changes should have serum potassium levels lowered quickly. C
Patients with hyperkalemia and characteristic ECG changes should be given intravenous calcium. C
Patients requiring urgent management should be treated with inhaled albuterol (salbutamol), insulin-glucose, or both as well as with loop diuretics. B
Total body potassium should be lowered with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, but this should not be the sole therapy in patients requiring urgent management, because it takes at least 4 hours to work. B
Use potassium binders and dietary strategies to maintain evidence-based cardiovascular and renal therapies whenever possible.
Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting results of diagnostic tests once life-threatening hyperkalemia has been diagnosed and samples of blood and urine for tests have been collected.

If hyperkalemia is identified by routine testing in a patient who is asymptomatic and whose rise in serum potassium is thought to be gradual rather than sudden (example, gradual increase in a patient with chronic renal failure), then outpatient therapy with polystyrene sulfonate (usual dose 15 g dissolved in water up to four times daily) can be considered even in patients with serum potassium over 6.0 mEq/L.

Risk factors such as acidosis, sudden onset of hyperkalemia, levels of potassium over 6.0 mEq/L, symptoms such as weakness or mental status changes, or ECG changes indicate that inpatient management is usually appropriate, generally in a monitored setting.
In-hospital management should proceed according to the algorithm ().

If serum potassium is over 6.0 mEq/L and the patient is unstable clinically, or ECG changes are present, intravenous calcium (10-20 ml of a 10% solution) should be given intravenously over 2 to 3 minutes. ECG changes should correct in 2 to 3 minutes. Calcium is cardioprotective but has no effect on serum potassium levels. The use of intravenous calcium in patients on digitalis therapy could theoretically increase digitalis toxicity. For this reason, some experts recommend giving intravenous calcium more slowly (over 30 minutes) in patients with hyperkalemia on digitalis, or using intravenous magnesium as an alternative.

Therapy with polystyrene sulfonate can be initiated on admission but should not be the sole therapy for ill patients; beta-agonists and/or insulin/glucose should be given as indicated in the algorithm ().

However, sodium polystyrene sulfonate use in elderly patients is associated with a higher risk of hospitalization for serious adverse gastrointestinal (GI) events, particularly intestinal ischemia or thrombosis.
Use of loop diuretics (for example, furosemide 20-40 mg intravenously) will increase renal potassium excretion and can be used along with the above-mentioned modalities.

Patiromer (Veltassa) has been FDA approved to treat acute hyperkalemia. It exhanges potassium for calcium in the gut. However it is not indicated as emergency therapy for life-threatening hyperkalemia because of delayed onset.

Long-term management includes addressing reversible causes of hyperkalemia, reviewing medications, and implementing dietary modification. In patients receiving renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors for heart failure or chronic kidney disease, efforts should be made to maintain evidence-based therapy when possible, including use of diuretics or potassium binders to control recurrent hyperkalemia.

For stable outpatients with diabetes, mild chronic renal failure, and recurrent episodes of hyperkalemia, the diagnosis of hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism should be considered. If a therapeutic trial of fludrocortisone 0.1 mg p.o. daily resolves the hyperkalemia, this diagnosis can be empirically assumed. Therapy with fludrocortisone may be needed chronically or intermittently. Side effects are rare, but hypertension or fluid retention, which can be corrected with diuretics, occurs occasionally.

The use of bicarbonate in the acute setting for hyperkalemia is no longer recommended. However, hyperkalemia associated with angiotensin-converting enzyme or angiotensin receptor blocker use in the outpatient setting may respond to therapy with sodium bicarbonate tablets, two 8 mEq tablets, or a half teaspoon of baking soda. Generally, diuretics should also be given to avoid fluid overload.

In an RCT of 753 patients with hyperkalemia, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) significantly reduced serum potassium compared with placebo within 48 hours and maintained normokalemia for up to 12 days.

For chronic hyperkalemia, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer are preferred potassium binders because they are generally better tolerated than sodium polystyrene sulfonate and may facilitate continuation of guideline-directed RAAS inhibitor therapy.

Among 237 outpatients with hyperkalemia (serum potassium levels >5.1 mEq/L) ZS-9 was associated with a sustained decrease in serum potassium (<5.1 mEq/L) in 80% to 94% of treated patients vs 46% for placebo. However, hypokalemia developed in about 10% of treated patients compared to none in the placebo group.

However sodium zirconium cyclosilicate showed similar reductions in serum potassium as sodium polystyrene sulfonate is a study of emergency department patients presenting with hyperkalemia (-1.1 mEq/L for both groups).

Among patients in whom adrenal insufficiency was diagnosed as the cause of their hyperkalemia, treatment should be initiated with hydrocortisone (20-35 mg daily given in 2 or 3 divided doses, the largest dose given in the AM, the second dose given 2 hours after lunch and the third dose given later in the afternoon) along with fludrocortisone (50-100 mcg daily).

Patiromer (Veltassa) is a potassium binding drug that exchanges potassium for calcium in the GI tract. In a randomized trial of 878 patients with systolic heart failure and a history of RAAS inhibitor associated hyperkalemia, patients were randomized to patiromer or placebo. Risk of hyperkalemia > 5.5 mmol/L was significantly lower with patiromer (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.45-0.87).
Outpatient followup of patients with hyperkalemia involves removing risk factors and education regarding a low-potassium diet. C
Patients with the combination of diabetes, mild chronic renal failure, and recurrent hyperkalemia may have hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. This will respond to treatment with oral fludrocortisone. C
Patients should be advised regarding foods and medications that might predispose them to hyperkalemia.
Patients at risk for hyperkalemia should be advised to keep hydrated and contact their physician when they are ill.

cell.label: Is potassium level more than 6.0 mEq/L (6.0 mmol/L), or are electrocardiograph (ECG) changes present?
Give insulin with glucose and/or albuterol (Ventolin) by nebulizer.
Order tests: spot urine potassium, osmolality, creatinine.
Repeat insulin and glucose; consider hemodialysis.
Give sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) or furosemide (Lasix).
